💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that temperatures are starting to rise, with some parts of the US facing a record-setting early heat wave this week.
  • That’s the major takeaway from new research published in the journal Neurology: The study uncovered three lesser-known factors that can trigger migraine—and these triggers can crop up even more in the late spring and summer.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you’re one of the 12% of Americans who deals with these headaches, this is information to keep in your back pocket.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that temperatures are starting to rise, with some parts of the US facing a record-setting early heat wave this week. But while you’re probably focused on staying cool, there’s one more thing that should be on your radar: a higher-than-usual risk of migraine headaches.

That’s the major takeaway from new research published in the journal Neurology: The study uncovered three lesser-known factors that can trigger migraine—and these triggers can crop up even more in the late spring and summer.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re one of the 12% of Americans who deals with these headaches, this is information to keep in your back pocket. Here’s what the study found, plus how doctors who treat patients with migraine recommend protecting yourself.

For the study, researchers followed 7,032 people living in Israel for about a decade who suffered from migraines. During the study period, researchers looked at participants’ daily exposure to air pollution, along with tracking weather conditions. They also looked at how often and when people visited the hospital or their primary care doctor with a migraine. That data was compared to the levels of pollution and weather conditions on that particular day, along with seven days before that.

During the study period, 2,215 people (or 32%) had at least one visit to the hospital or a clinic with a migraine. The researchers also found that 47% of participants in the study bought triptan medications at one point or another—fast-acting prescription medications that are designed to stop a migraine—with most using at least two tablets a month.

Sources indicate that ultimately, the researchers discovered a link between three weather-related factors and migraine: air pollution, temperature (including UV exposure), and humidity. First, they found a correlation between higher levels of air pollution and the most number of visits to a hospital or clinic for a migraine. They also found that the day with the least visits to the hospital or clinic also had lower-than-average pollution levels. People with short-term exposure to high levels of nitrogen dioxide (a common pollutant from traffic exhaust) were 41% more likely to go to the hospital or clinic for migraine than people who weren’t exposed to high levels of the gas.

According to recent reports, the study also indicated that people who were exposed to high levels of UV rays from the sun on a given day were 23% more likely to visit a healthcare provider for migraine symptoms than those who weren’t. High temperatures and low humidity appear to be linked to more migraine headaches, likely because they amplify the effect of nitrogen dioxide, the researchers mentioned.

With climate change intensifying how often we deal with heat waves and pollution, it’s key to consider these risk factors when it comes to migraine, the researchers wrote.

In a recent development, it’s important to note that the study didn’t prove that air pollution, heat, and lower humidity levels cause migraines—it just found a link between them. But doctors say there’s likely something here.

Industry observers note that air pollution can spark neuroinflammation (the immune system’s inflammatory response in the brain and spinal cord), which is a risk factor for migraine, Sana Ghafoor, MD, neurologist at Tufts Medical Center, tells SELF. This may cause a release of pain chemicals like calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and substance P that can lead to a migraine, Dr. Ghafoor indicates.

Industry observers note that air pollution may be particularly problematic for people with allergies who also struggle with migraines, Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, California, tells SELF. The body may see air pollution as an allergen and mount an immune response, which can spark a migraine in people who are sensitive to this trigger, he explains.

Sources indicate that then, there’s the fact that heat can impact blood vessels and nerves. “When people heat up, nerves and blood vessels in tight locations can become irritated, as the diameter of a blood vessel or nerves increases with heat,” Dr. Segil states. That, too, can trigger a migraine. You’re also more susceptible to getting dehydrated when it’s hot out, Dr. Ghafoor says: “If you're overheated and dehydrated, those can also trigger migraines.”.

In a recent development, dr. Segil points out that high humidity common in the spring and summer (and not just that related to air pollution) can trigger migraines too. High humidity causes you to sweat and lose water, which can decrease the amount of blood in your blood vessels (if you don’t replace it), Dr. Segil states. “This decreases the diameter of blood vessels and can cause headaches, just like an increased blood vessel diameter,” he says.

Dr. Ghafoor claims she often sees more patients have migraine headaches when high humidity strikes. “Even with small [atmospheric] pressure changes, it can activate nerve endings and sinuses, which can lead to the release of pain chemicals,” she says.

These are some of the most common migraine triggers, according to the US National Library of Medicine:.

These foods and ingredients can also trigger migraines, per the US National Library of Medicine:.

Industry observers note that migraine triggers are personal, making it notable to do what you can to figure out yours and then try to avoid them as best as possible. (Dr. Ghafoor recommends keeping a headache diary to try to narrow things down.) But factors like air pollution, heat, and humidity can be tough to avoid.

It has been revealed that if levels of air pollution are high in your area, Dr. Segil recommends wearing a face mask like an N95 when you need to be outdoors. Keeping your windows shut and running an air purifier can also help tamp down on pollution indoors. If you’d like, you can track pollution levels throughout the day and try to stay inside during peak times, Dr. Ghafoor indicates.

When heat and humidity strikes, Dr. Ghafoor recommends doing what you can to stay well hydrated. “Make sure that it’s not just water, but electrolytes too,” she says. “All of that is a very important part of lifestyle management for patients who have migraine.”.

Industry observers note that ultimately, doing your best to try to figure out your triggers (and avoid them) can go a long way toward helping to keep you more comfortable on a regular basis. “Knowing and identifying migraine triggers is very important,” Dr. Ghafoor says. “It’s empowering the patient to understand their disease.”.

#91903. After Losing My Son, I Didn't Want to Be ‘Strong’

After Losing My Son, I Didn't Want to Be ‘Strong’

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that during my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal.
  • At the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy.
  • If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that during my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal. It was sharp, persistent, and unsettling in a way I couldn’t ignore. As a former labor and delivery nurse, I understood the risks in a way many patients do not. I knew what to watch for. I knew my history. I knew when something felt wrong. Yet when I raised concerns, they were not met with the urgency they deserved.

At the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy. I knew that the vertical incision on my uterus could put a future pregnancy at risk. I spoke up. I asked questions. I paid attention to my body. Still, when I experienced a uterine rupture, I was navigating a system that did not respond with the level of care and urgency that the moment required.

If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?

Conversations during Black Maternal Health Week often center around one urgent truth: Black women are still far more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes in this country than white women. This is not an assumption. It is a proven fact, and it should stop all of us in our tracks. It also does not only impact one socioeconomic group. It affects everyone, including some of the most visible and resourced women in the world.

As the founder of Mielle, my mission is to empower women, especially Black women, to express their authentic selves. At its core, that mission is about care, agency, and visibility, which is why conversations like this matter. It’s about showing up for every part of Black women’s experience. We need to talk more candidly about what happens to Black women who survive the trauma of miscarriage or stillbirth, and the prolonged mental health challenges that can follow, including postpartum depression.

Sources indicate that black women are expected to remain “strong” while navigating medical emergencies. We’re dismissed, told to wait, to calm down, and to trust a system that has not always earned that trust. We survive experiences that change our families and us forever. And then, too often, we are expected to do something just as impossible: keep going as if survival is the end of the story. It is not.

That is why Black Maternal Health Week cannot be about mortality alone. It must also be about what it means to live after trauma, preventable harm, and loss that reshapes your life.

The data make clear that this crisis is ongoing. Black women are about three times more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes than white women, and more than 80% of those deaths are considered preventable. Black infants also die at more than twice the rate of white infants. These are not random gaps. They reflect a healthcare system and a culture that too often normalizes Black women’s pain instead of responding to it.

Research demonstrates that one in five women, or about 20%, report mistreatment during maternity care, but for Black women, that figure climbs to nearly 30%, reflecting more frequent experiences of bias, disrespect, and lack of autonomy in clinical settings. Nearly half of women say they have held back from asking questions or sharing concerns. In one of the most vulnerable moments of a person’s life, too many are already calculating whether speaking up will make things worse.

In a recent development, in my own life, grief did not arrive quietly. It entered my marriage, my motherhood, my body, my faith, and eventually my work. In my book, The Glory In Your Story, I write about how grief does not follow a timeline. It becomes part of who you are, and healing begins not by outrunning it, but by acknowledging it.

Recent findings suggest that that matters because so many Black women are praised for being strong when what we actually need is space to be human. After losing Milan, I returned to work. I kept moving. I built Mielle. From the outside, it can look like a story of resilience. And in many ways, it is. But we have to be honest about the lessons we take from stories like mine.

Industry observers note that the lesson should not be that Black women are uniquely equipped to carry devastating grief and still perform at a high level. It should not be that our resilience makes systemic failures acceptable. And it should not be that we have to turn survival into something productive just to make our pain legible.

Too often, we celebrate the comeback without sitting long enough with the conditions that made it necessary.

Faith carried me. Purpose helped me rebuild. But none of that changes the reality that more listening, better care, stronger hospital systems, and greater urgency might have changed my story. If we are serious about maternal health, we have to be just as serious about saying that clearly.

Sources indicate that black Maternal Health Week gives us an opportunity to think more broadly about what justice looks like. It looks like hospitals are equipped for emergencies. It looks like providers who listen to Black women the first time, without requiring patients to fight to be believed. It looks like support for families after loss–not just during a crisis. And it looks like making space for grief without expecting Black women to turn it into inspiration before we are ready.

It’s time that we honor not only the women we have lost, but also the women still here carrying what the system could not or would not hold for them. Survival is not the finish line. Being heard, protected, and cared for should be.

It has been revealed that mexico-based COLECTIVO C733 was named the inaugural recipient of the Siza Award for public architecture, established by the Serralves Foundation. The first edition marks the 10th anniversary of the Serralves Foundation's Álvaro Siza Archive and aims to recognize architectural generosity and public-space engagement, in honor of the Portuguese architect's vision. Like Siza's body of work, the award is open to the international community. COLECTIVO C733's public infrastructure portfolio includes markets, cultural facilities, transport hubs and public landscapes across Mexico, such as Bacalar Eco-Park, Guadalupe Market, Tapachula Station, Nacajuca's Music House community center and Matamoros Market, as well as their work with Mexico's Ministry of Agrarian, Territorial and Urban Development (SEDATU) in vulnerable regions and along the U.S.–Mexico border.

It places special emphasis on architectural generosity and targets emerging practices and architects in their thirties and forties with demonstrated sensitivity to local communities, territory, and the environment. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Side stitch, stomach cramp, side ache — whatever you wanna call it, that mid-run pain in your tum can seriously *cramp* your runner’s high.

It has been revealed that this pesky prob that plagues runners and athletes all over has a scientific name: Exercise-related transient abdominal pain (ETAP). Though experts don’t know exactly what causes it, they have some ideas and tips about how to stop it.

Before you double-over during your next marathon, here’s what to know.

That fateful stab in your side is most likely to happen during exercise where your upper bod indicates tight and upright for an extended period, such as when you run, jog, bike, hike, play soccer, etc.

Recent findings suggest that this common prob has been around for ages — the first historical mention is from ancient Roman philosopher Pliny the Elder. Yet, scientists still haven’t reached a consensus on its exact cause. We know that it affects up to 70% of runners each year.

It’s also more likely to occur on the right side.

A stiff spine or poor posture (according to older research from 2010) could contribute to side stitches – but TBH, the pros don’t know for sure.

According to a 2022 review, researchers also think a side stitch might be caused by your right foot hitting the ground while you breathe out, irritating a phrenic nerve. Researchers think this, in turn, may bother the lining of your abdomen (particularly on the lower right side). Since most people are right-foot dominant, this is one possible explanation.

Experts also theorize that it could be triggered by the boost of blood flow around the diaphragm when running.

Furthermore, fueling up before a big race is excellent — but eating or drinking large quantities right before running may boost your risk of getting a side stitch, anecdotal reports suggest.

When a side stitch strikes, don’t stress – there are steps you can take, including:.

To stop a side stitch before it begins, here are some ideas FTW:.

Side stitches are usually harmless. But it’s always a good idea to visit a pro if you experience any of the following probs:.

Side stitches are a common issue and not typically the reason for concern. Though pros don’t know what causes them, they think issues with breathing, posture, or nerves may play a role.

It has been revealed that consider working on your running form or breathing to reduce the risk of experiencing a side stitch. Staying hydrated and avoiding huge meals pre-run may also help. Consider working with a physical therapist or personal trainer if your complications persist.

If you experience pain under your breastbone when running, visit a doctor asap.

#91899. Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on.
  • In a recent development, if you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone.
  • There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on. But these symptoms, as vague as they are, could actually stem from a health condition that’s historically been deemed a “male disease”: obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA.

In a recent development, if you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone. It wasn’t until the ’90s that researchers first recognized that OSA, which causes you to repeatedly stop breathing while asleep, often presents differently in women than it does in men. For starters women with the condition may not even snore.

There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.

Industry observers note that “The disease itself was defined in men,” explains Jennifer Martin, PhD, a behavioral sleep medicine specialist and professor at Florida International University’s Herbert Wertheim College of Medicine in Miami. “The way men and women breathe when they’re asleep is not the same, and our definition of the disease doesn’t account for that.”.

Recent findings suggest that although obstructive sleep apnea appears to be less common and typically milder in women (at least before menopause), studies suggest that the consequences of the disease, if left untreated, can be similar, if not worse, for us, making it vital to learn the signs and seek help. Here’s what we know about obstructive sleep apnea and its impact on women. Plus, experts explain how to advocate for the best care if you think you may have the condition.

Sleep apnea is one of several conditions that fall under the sleep-disordered breathing umbrella. The most common type is OSA, which happens when your upper airway repeatedly collapses during sleep, making it harder for air to reach your lungs, claims Anita Valanju Shelgikar, MD, a sleep medicine physician with University of Michigan Health and president of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

The textbook symptoms of this condition—which, for the record, were determined based on studies mostly involving men—include loud snoring and dramatic gasps for air as a person tries to continue breathing while asleep. But this often isn’t the case for women, Dr. Shelgikar tells SELF. Instead, women with OSA are more likely to have nightmares, wake up multiple times a night, have trouble staying asleep, and deal with insomnia, which then causes symptoms like daytime fatigue, morning headaches, and mood swings. Women also have more hypopneas (shallow breaths with less oxygen flow), whereas men tend toward apneas (complete pauses in breathing).

In a recent development, some experts speculate that it’s possible snoring isn’t commonly reported among women with this disorder because they’re embarrassed to talk about it, given society expects them to sleep like Disney princesses. But a growing body of research suggests that biology may better explain this and other sex-related differences in symptoms. For example, compared with men, women have smaller, more stable airways that are less likely to collapse (and in turn vibrate, making you snore) during sleep. Women also tend to have less fat around their necks, and before menopause they seemingly benefit from the protective effects of estrogen and progesterone, which interact with the respiratory system in a way that aids breathing.

Sources indicate that all things considered, it makes sense why more men than women in the US have this condition, making up about 59% and 41% of obstructive sleep apnea patients, respectively. However, once women go through menopause, which causes their estrogen and progesterone levels to drop, the rate of OSA and the severity of symptoms in this group increases dramatically, Dr. Martin notes. Studies have found that anywhere from 47% to 67% of postmenopausal women have obstructive sleep apnea, which is about the same as men in this age range (50 and older). The number of women who actually get diagnosed with the condition is a different story, though—more on that shortly.

It has been revealed that regardless of age, however, women still deal with more sleep apnea–related symptoms than men, Dr. Martin adds, even if they have a less severe form of the condition. This is likely because women have more “subtle breathing disturbances” during sleep that hurt the overall quality of their rest compared with men, Dr. Martin claims.

It has been revealed that because women often don’t experience “classic” OSA symptoms, they end up being misdiagnosed or dismissed. “When [men] walk into a physician’s office and say they’re sleepy and they snore, they get a diagnostic test right away,” Dr. Martin claims. “When a woman walks in and says, ‘I don’t sleep well, and I’m very fatigued during the day,’ they don’t often get referred” for screening. In fact, research suggests that men are nine times more likely to be referred for diagnostic testing than women.

Recent findings suggest that women with OSA commonly have their symptoms misattributed to conditions like depression, anxiety, insomnia, and menopause or even medication side effects, indicates Dr. Shelgikar, who is also a neurology professor at the University of Michigan Medical School. Not to mention women can have these other conditions as well, which might make their sleep apnea not only harder to detect but also worsen it. Take the double whammy that is insomnia and OSA: Having both of these disorders at the same time is more common among women than men, Dr. Martin says, and in some cases they may be given a sleep aid (such as diphenhydramine or a benzodiazepine) that can further relax their throat muscles, exacerbating their sleep apnea and leaving them even more oxygen-deprived.

And it doesn’t help that, as we talked about earlier, the diagnostic criteria for OSA are largely based on how the condition presents in men. “When we diagnose sleep apnea, we require one of two things to happen: A breathing interruption has to be associated either with a drop in oxygen levels or a brief awakening from sleep,” Dr. Martin says. “Women don’t have those very deep drops in oxygen levels that men do. So that means that the way we define the disease itself kind of biases us towards diagnosing it more in men than women.” What’s more, Medicare, which the vast majority of Americans ages 65 and older rely on for health insurance, only recognizes a sleep apnea diagnosis if a person has those steep drops in oxygen, Dr. Martin says. Those typical mid-slumber wake-ups don’t count on their own. So even “the criteria that Medicare forces people to use to define sleep apnea is very male-centric,” she adds.

In a recent development, home sleep apnea tests, which are becoming increasingly common as a cheaper alternative to the gold standard in-lab exams, are also more prone to miss the condition in women. Because women tend to have fewer and milder events than men, these at-home tests may not be able to diagnose sleep apnea as accurately in this population, Dr. Martin states. They can be even more inaccurate in women with insomnia. These individuals “may not get enough sleep to get an accurate diagnosis,” she says, “so if they wear [the monitor] for six hours, but they’re only sleeping for four of them, it may look like they have less sleep apnea than they really do.”.

In a recent development, that’s all to say that sleep apnea is likely much more common among women than the available data suggests, experts tell SELF. And that reality reveals a sobering point: A lot of women with this condition probably aren’t receiving the care they need, a delay that can, for some people, snowball into an avalanche of additional yet preventable health concerns.

If left untreated, sleep apnea can have downstream effects on your health, particularly your heart, claims Atul Malhotra, MD, research chief of pulmonary, critical care, and sleep medicine at UC San Diego Health. Every time you stop breathing, your body responds to the lack of oxygen by releasing the stress hormone adrenaline to jolt you awake so you take a breath. This happens really quickly; you are typically up for just a few seconds and probably won’t even remember it the next morning.

Over time this constant stress strains your cardiovascular system, Dr. Malhotra says, which may increase your risk for high blood pressure, heart attack, stroke, irregular heartbeat, and heart failure. Although the evidence is mixed, some research suggests that it’s more common for women with severe sleep apnea to experience cardiovascular complications than it is for men. Studies also show that women tend to have more health conditions upon diagnosis than men do, including thyroid disease, asthma, and depression. This raises the classic “chicken or the egg” question, but either way treating OSA can only help.

Industry observers note that because obstructive sleep apnea leads to low-quality shut-eye, it is also associated with memory and cognition problems and poor daytime alertness, which can boost the likelihood of car and workplace accidents (for certain high-risk jobs like those in the transportation and construction industries), Dr. Shelgikar claims. Perhaps less discussed is how untreated sleep apnea affects our ability to care for ourselves and maintain relationships. “We don’t do a good job thinking about sleep apnea as a potential cause of mental health symptoms,” Dr. Martin says. In fact, research shows that managing OSA could actually help some people dealing with anxiety and depression improve their symptoms.

As researchers continue searching for answers, Dr. Martin points to a silver lining: There’s good evidence to suggest that women “benefit at least as much as men, if not more” from sleep apnea treatment, which is why it’s vital to know what to look out for.

Although you’re quite literally working against decades of medical bias, it’s still possible to receive a sleep apnea diagnosis if you’re equipped with the right intel.

Tech Report: Programa software tracks everything from product dimensions to material quantities

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (597 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Studio operations software Programa has redesigned its programme to rethink how interior design studios operate, giving practices more flexibility and freeing up their time.
  • According to Programa, beautiful interiors are built on “hundreds of decisions”, which take long periods of time to decide upon and update across multiple spreadsheets.
  • Each decision brings specification details, quantities, pricing and revisions that studios must keep updated as a project develops.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Studio operations software Programa has redesigned its programme to rethink how interior design studios operate, giving practices more flexibility and freeing up their time.

According to Programa, beautiful interiors are built on “hundreds of decisions”, which take long periods of time to decide upon and update across multiple spreadsheets.

Each decision brings specification details, quantities, pricing and revisions that studios must keep updated as a project develops.

These include minute, precise details such as dimensions, materials, finishes, technical requirements, and component quantities.

Programa‘s redesigned programme keeps a record of each item used in an interior project, from furniture and lighting to hardware and finishes, and optimises their organisation based on how the project runs.

The manufacturer explained that increased AI use is making convincing images “easier to generate than ever”, yet clients often run into logistical problems when using this alone.

For example, the AI model doesn’t take into account whether a wardrobe or sofa fits through the door, suits the needs of the people living there, or whether the overall design takes full advantage of a space’s natural light.

With Programa, the designer can smoothly make these judgements using the software’s organisation of specifications, cost, quantities and overall project coordination.

The manufacturer explained that if a designer updates a product’s shared specification once, the change appears in the Programa schedules that include it, while quantities can be individually allocated by room.

For Austin Carrier of Californian design studio, Hommeboys Interiors, this is particularly helpful.

“We use schedules for everything from lighting and hardware to plumbing fixtures and furniture, indoor and outdoor,” Carrier explained.

“For furniture, we can break down every room, then the pieces within that room, and give clients several options to reject or accept,” he added.

As a result, the software aims to cut the “gruelling amount of work” updating schedules, preparing presentations, and communicating with suppliers. It also reduces repeated data entry, freeing up time.

The platform is defined as an “alternative to spreadsheets”, which often have to be made from scratch and reformatted for different presentations.

“The problem with the spreadsheet is that it’s like a blank cell,” added Los Angeles-based designer Paul Chan. “You can put anything in there – it doesn’t carry from one project to another.”.

“With Programa, I can take a format from one project and move it into the next,” Chan continued. “There’s consistency between each project.”.

Specifically, the Programa Schedule function details the items’ code, supplier, finish, dimensions, quantity and price.

It offers a streamlined place to reference drawings, get client approval and work with contractors to meet on-site deadlines.

The company explained that one of its platform’s main benefits is that it can be used from early product decision-making through to final delivery.

According to recent reports, here, the studio manages the specification and controls what is shared, whereas the clients review selections and provide approvals. Collaborators also receive the information relevant to their work.

“Once we get all of the information in there, we can send it out in one email to all of our vendors, and then they are able to get us pricing back very easily,” added Tana Nesbitt-Hayes of Studio 8 Architect.

Magnesium is found in fatty fish, leafy greens, whole grains — and the supplement aisle.

The mighty mineral plays many essential roles in our bodies, but can it help tighten the belt buckle?

We checked in with a doctor to find out.

While magnesium can sneakily support weight loss in a few ways, that’s not its main gig.

“Magnesium alone is not a magic bullet for weight loss,” says Paunel Vukasinov, MD, a dual board-certified internist and obesity medicine specialist with Medical Offices of Manhattan.

“A comprehensive approach including diet, exercise, and other lifestyle changes are essential,” Vukasinov adds.

Here are a few ways magnesium may support weight loss, as explained by Vukasinov.

“Magnesium is not classified as an appetite suppressant,” Vukasinov says.

“However, by potentially stabilizing blood sugar and insulin levels, magnesium may reduce cravings and help prevent overeating. This effect can indirectly support weight loss.”.

Vukasinov reminds us that no specific magnesium dosage is prescribed solely for fat loss.

With that in mind, the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for magnesium is:.

Vukasinov notes that sticking to the RDA ensures you meet your body’s needs without over-supplementing.

“Excessive intake does not enhance weight loss and may lead to adverse effects,” he adds.

According to Vukasinov, it’s best to get magnesium from food since a nutrient-dense diet, including whole foods, boosts your intake of other extra essentials like fiber, which improves overall health.

Here are some foods you can gobble up for the most magnesium:.

If you know your diet isn’t cutting it, you can find magnesium supplements at major retailers, like Wal-Mart and Target, drug stores, or Amazon.

PSA: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not check the safety or effectiveness of dietary supplements, so it’s notable to choose a reputable brand that undertakes third-party testing to prove the purity and quality of their products.

For some, magnesium supplements may cause a few unsavory side effects, including diarrhea, stomach upset, or cramping.

According to recent reports, remember that there are many forms of magnesium. Vukasinov points out that magnesium citrate or magnesium oxide can have a laxative effect (yikes).

Be sure you’re taking the best dose based on your RDA, and consider taking it with a meal to better avoid side effects.

Magnesium is not a miracle solution for weight loss, but getting enough of it can ensure that your body produces enough energy and gets enough sleep — both play a significant hand in weight management.

Taking too much will have you gripping your belly with stomach pain or diarrhea, so stick to the daily recommended amounts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A single-use earplug crafted from seaweed, two plant-based insulation materials and a homegrown timber kit-of-parts for low-rise buildings are among the projects that have been awarded Design Museum grants.

UK-based studios Searo Labs, WeCanMake, Local Works Studio and SY Ecofit have been granted a share of £280,000 from the Design Museum for their “cutting-edge” environmental prototypes.

Described as the “world’s first seaweed-based single-use earplug”, SearoSoft by Cambridge-based Searo Labs is a fully biodegradable and renewable alternative to single-use earplugs.

According to SearoSoft, the soft, mouldable earplugs are made without microplastics or chemicals and designed to hydrate the ear canal, unlike plastic-based products, which can be drying.

Sources indicate that once discarded, they are biodegradable in water or soil after 30 days. As seaweed is a regenerative crop, SearoSoft explained that there is no need for land, freshwater or fertilisers, making the process simple and more sustainable.

Sources indicate that among the other prototypes is a building material project by Sussex-based Local Works Studio. The initiative, named Ferment, will repurpose agricultural waste into an insulating material fit for retrofitting buildings.

Local Works Studio aims to develop an accessible product for farms via what it calls a “harvest-to-house system”, where farmers can produce the insulation themselves using their existing infrastructure, skills and machinery.

Bristol-based studio WeCanMake’s winning prototype, Neighbourhood Factory Futures, is a homegrown timber kit-of-parts system designed to be used for constructing low-rise apartment buildings.

With the Design Museum’s grant, the studio plans to create a neighbourhood factory model, allowing local communities to build and maintain their own homes.

WeCanMake explained it created the system as part of a wider movement aiming to make the UK a “nation of growers, producers and makers” while using reusable materials that store, rather than emit, carbon.

Prototyping PhytoFloc by social enterprise SY Ecofit in collaboration with Phyona and Studio Bio is a zero-waste project that, similarly to Local Works Studio, aims to develop plant-based insulation for building construction.

The project uses biowaste created as a byproduct of phytomining, where former industrial land is rejuvenated by plants that extract pollutants from the soil.

The project intends to recognise the value of post-industrial soils while creating a locally made, low-carbon material.

Sources indicate that the grants are part of the Design Museum’s Future Observatory program, which is run in partnership with the Arts and Humanities Research Council. The winning projects were amongst 140 prototypes that were submitted to the scheme.

The museum explained that at a time when supply chains are under pressure, the Future Observatory aims to support designers’ practical research to drive the green transition.

“The climate crisis demands rapid change, and we believe that design is critically crucial if we are to meet that challenge,” mentioned Design Museum director Tim Marlow.

“The presence of Future Observatory allows us an extraordinary opportunity to get involved with practitioners and problem-solvers and have a direct impact on the development of new technologies at the frontier of current design thinking.”.

According to recent reports, the four projects will be funded from November 2026 until July 2027. Afterwards, the prototypes will be tested and begin the commercialisation process.

Images courtesy of Waugh Thistleton Architects.

UK studio Waugh Thistleton Architects is set to transform the Edwardian Westbrook Pavilion in Margate, UK, into an arts centre for British artist Tracey Emin with a cafe, public sauna and changing rooms.

“The project will bring a much-loved seafront building back into use, combining its original purpose with newly introduced spaces for art, culture and the local community,” mentioned Waugh Thistleton Architects.

The studio recently won planning permission from the local council to convert the abandoned building, which Emin purchased in 2023, into a facility run by the Tracey Emin Foundation.

The project aims to return the building to its former use as a changing room for swimmers and as a tea room, when it originally opened in 1914.

“Originally opened in 1914, the building provided public changing facilities for sea-bathing and a tea room,” said the studio.

“Following storm damage in the Great North Sea Storm of 1953, subsequent alterations detracted from its original Edwardian character,” it continued.

“The renovated pavilion will accommodate artist studios, an art gallery, clubroom, cafe, sea-bathing changing facilities, a fresh sauna and refurbished public toilets, restoring its original role as a place for bathing and socialising by the sea.”.

Recent findings suggest that along with making the pavilion a building used by the public again, the studio aims to return the building’s core to its Edwardian look by removing later additions. It will also add glazed facades to the wings on either side of the central pavilion.

The building will be topped by a rooftop terrace, while a public toilet on the site will be renovated.

“The design draws on the proportions and character of the original building, removing later additions and reinstating lost features such as the historic belvederes which top the central tower structures,” remarked the studio.

“The beachfront facade will see a newly introduced glazing system and colonnade to each of the building’s wings, with a new sheltered archway forming a new seating terrace at the building’s heart,” it continued.

“The design seeks to reference the original architecture while providing contemporary needs of a public building. Where original features are references, these are distinguishable architecturally.”.

Emin is one of the UK’s best-known living artists. We recently produced a video of a landmark exhibition of her work at Tate Modern.

Recent projects by Waugh Thistleton Architects include plans for the “tallest mass timber office building in the US”.

Picture this: you've just landed in Honolulu after a long transcontinental flight. You've got four days on Maui planned, and then a few nights on Kauai before heading home. The problem? Those interisland flights add up fast — Hawaiian Airlines will gladly charge you $150–$250 *per person* for a 20-to-40-minute hop between islands. For a family of four, that's easily $600–$1,000 in airfare just to island-hop, on top of everything else you've already spent to get to Hawaii. Now imagine paying 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person instead — miles you transferred from your American Express Membership Rewards account at a 1:1 ratio just a day or two before booking. Suddenly, that $150–$250 ticket costs you points worth less than a nice dinner. At 3.3 cents per point on the high end, you're extracting extraordinary value from miles that most people leave sitting in an account doing nothing. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about finding pricing inefficiencies in loyalty programs. Hawaiian Airlines prices these interisland segments on a dynamic award chart — but because these are short, regional hops operated almost entirely on 717s and A321s between islands most people aren't cross-shopping for redemptions, the program hasn't inflated the price the way major international carriers have. The sweet spot holds. The math is simple and satisfying: a cash ticket from Honolulu (HNL) to Kahului, Maui (OGG) or Lihue, Kauai (LIH) typically runs $100–$250. You're redeeming 7,500 miles to cover that cost, which means you're getting **1.3 to 3.3 cents per point** in value — above what most programs deliver on domestic redemptions. And because Hawaiian charges **zero fuel surcharges** on its own-operated flights, every mile goes toward the ticket price, not toward fees. For the FI-minded traveler who planned a multi-island Hawaii trip anyway, this redemption doesn't just save money — it reframes how you think about points. These aren't bonuses. They're a currency, and knowing where to spend them is the skill.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: HawaiianMiles prices interisland flights at a flat 7,500 miles in economy, and that price is shockingly stable relative to what these tickets actually cost in cash.

It has been revealed that here's why this works as a pricing inefficiency. Hawaiian Airlines operates a near-monopoly on interisland travel in Hawaii. There's limited true competition for these routes (go! Mokulele operates turboprops on some routes, but Hawaiian dominates the jet service). Because cash demand is inelastic — visitors need to get between islands — Hawaiian charges a premium in cash. But the HawaiianMiles award program hasn't kept pace with those cash price increases in the same aggressive way that programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles have. The result: 7,500 miles per segment, consistently, while cash prices climb.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Shigeru Ban Architects.

A cross-shaped roof will mark the San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex in Rome, Italy, which Japanese studio Shigeru Ban Architects is designing with local architect Vittorio Petrucci.

The church will occupy a right now underused site in Ostia, a coastal neighbourhood for which the project is hoped to become an architectural landmark.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be constructed with a frame of timber – Ban’s signature material – with a deliberately simple form that is intended to evoke a fabric tent.

According to Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci, the overarching goal is for the church to help establish a greater sense of community and place in the area, which they describe as having a “fragmented urban fabric”.

“We wanted to design a place of worship that also brings the whole community together,” remarked Ban.

“The timber structure expresses the idea of a tent, a simple, welcoming form that connects people with one another and with their surroundings. Through this project, we hope architecture can help create a upcoming sense of belonging in the neighbourhood.”.

Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci’s proposal was the winning entry of a competition for the church.

It is one of five winning designs selected as part of the New Churches Programme – an initiative led by the local church district, the Diocese of Rome, and the Italian Episcopal Conference, an assembly of Catholic bishops, to provide permanent homes for parish communities in the region.

As part of the project, four new churches will be built, while one existing parish complex will be extended.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be built on a raised public plaza, with various parish facilities, community spaces and a priest’s residence embedded below.

Its key feature will be its angular roof, which is shaped like a cross but not immediately readable as one. This is modelled on a latent cross – a feature in sacred architecture, in which a cross shape is integrated in the spatial design, without being clearly visible.

Inside, the church will have a diamond-shaped plan, with large stained-glass windows positioned in the four cardinal directions. They will be triangular in shape and feature designs modelled on neighbourhood street art.

The project will be complete with a landscaped park, as well as various recreational and sports facilities, which the studios said will “create opportunities for social interaction and everyday activities”.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex is not the first church project by Ban. Among his others is the landmark Cardboard Cathedral in Newly introduced Zealand, which is formed of 98 cardboard tubes combined with wood and polycarbonate. We named it the most significant building of 2013 in our list of the 25 most significant buildings of the 21st century.

Other Italian church proposals recently featured on Dezeen include Stefano Boeri Architetti’s design for the Ambrosian Monastery in Milan, which will have a sail-like roof form.

Images courtesy of Shigeru Ban Architects.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sabine Marcelis has nominated Swedish Girls as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project sponsored by Kohler. In this interview, we learn why the design duo deliberately play into stereotypes.

The steady emergence of Swedish Girls has not been lost on prolific Dutch designer Marcelis, who nominated the collective as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design over the next 20 years.

“I really like how they work with existing industrial production processes, yet the result very much speaks to the current culture,” Marcelis told Dezeen, explaining her selection.

Josefin Zachrisson and Mira Bergh run multidisciplinary studio Swedish Girls between Stockholm and Milan, creating furniture, installations and set design.

Sources indicate that the duo met during their studies at Sweden’s Beckmans College of Design, where they graduated in 2019. They bonded over a desire to make work “without hierarchies” and maintain creative control of the studio’s output, which they prefer to call their ever-expanding “universe”.

The Significant Bang for Swedish Girls was the selection of their collective’s tongue-in-cheek name, chosen after their first exhibition outing at Milan design week.

For experimental platform Alcova in 2021, Zachrisson and Bergh unveiled their ongoing metal rod Seats System project (pictured left).

Originally a single piece of modular seating without a defined front or back, the project has evolved into more metal pieces that follow the same design language, including a fruit bowl and a candle holder.

According to recent reports, “We overheard people talking about our furniture, asking who made it, and others were like, ‘ah, it was those Swedish girls’, and we felt a bit belittled by it,” recalled Zachrisson. The duo had previously made work under their own names.

Sources indicate that “The Swedish girl has obviously become a phenomenon,” added Bergh. “You know, blonde, sexy. But when we were talking about it, we also found it really funny because it’s so stereotypical. We thought we’d call ourselves Swedish Girls because everybody else was already calling us that.”.

Industry observers note that humour is intrinsic to Zachrisson and Bergh’s interdisciplinary practice. Even their website, admired by Marcelis, was playfully designed as a Swedish Girls-branded Google search engine. It is meant to look like the internet itself, complete with mock web pages listing each of the collective’s projects.

“We got the idea when we launched the name Swedish Girls,” the pair explained.

“A professor from Beckmans called and said that we should change our name because when she Googled ‘Swedish Girls’, the search result was not exactly art and design,” they added.

“We thought that was so funny and decided to make Google about us instead of changing our name.”.

Another of the duo’s wit-inflected projects is Only Fans, an installation presented at Gothenburg’s Röhsska design museum in 2024 during local music festival Way Out West.

Dubbed “a multidimensional art experience about fan culture” in all its forms, the installation included 25 electric fans, selected as a riff on adult content platform OnlyFans, where women are often the subject of scrutiny.

“The installation was interactive, so that visitors could stand in the middle of the fans in a hysterical storm,” said Bergh.

Our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things. But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life.

Alongside the fans, the collective presented seven laser-cut steel chairs emblazoned with I <3 Swedish Girls, along with a fanzine and female mannequins wearing “metal merch” designed by Zachrisson and Bergh.

“Our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things,” considered Zachrisson.

In a recent development, “But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life,” she continued. “It feels like a way to approach it that makes it accessible.”.

Industry observers note that “Sometimes it’s hard because we get these questions like, ‘are you a feminist?'” added the designer. “But it’s inherently political to be a woman moving through the world. Our work is just reacting to our reality.”.

The pair is keen to highlight that although they make furniture, “social values are always a starting point” for their projects.

“We really want to have a practice that feels purposeful,” stated Zachrisson, considering the significance of partnering with institutions like design museums.

“We’ve realised that showing work in public spaces is the most important thing,” she continued.

Industry observers note that “Especially because the materials and processes we use have become quite expensive. So we want to put our pieces in public spaces so that everyone can take part in some way.”.

“You meet all different kinds of people, and we talk to them and grow from it,” added Bergh.

Recent findings suggest that the hardest thing is to earn money. We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money.

Despite Swedish Girls’ various collaborations and recurring presence at Milan design week, seven years after leaving Beckmans, Bergh and Zachrisson continue to work in cafes and supermarkets to fund their design practice.

The duo are hyperaware of the difficulties faced by emerging creatives, especially those like themselves who, as they put it, “want to listen to your gut and be close to the process”.

Sources indicate that “The hardest thing is to earn money,” said Bergh. “We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money on very quick timelines. I feel like we should have more respect.”.

In a recent development, “You don’t get paid in a way where you as two people can survive,” added Zachrisson. “But all these years of working and keeping our creative integrity is paying off in every way except financially.”.

When it comes to building their studio, the designers consider themselves to be playing the long game.

“Long term, it’s an investment to do it this way because we have now created a context where we can feel freedom and gain respect, which is why we were so happy when Sabine nominated us,” stated Zachrisson.

“You can measure success in so many different ways and with this we feel respected, and that is so valuable.”.

The duo stated funding that they won from Sweden’s Konstnärsnämnden arts council after graduating gave them a significant leg up when they were just starting out.

Zachrisson and Bergh are concerned that scholarships like theirs have been scarcer across Sweden in recent years thanks to the country’s right-wing administration, which came into power in 2022 and has only just been voted out of office.

According to recent reports, “All the artists we have talked to have felt an extreme difference in that time,” noted Zachrisson. “The share of the total budget allocated to culture has not been this low in 26 years.”.

Still, the pair are confident and excited about what’s to come.

“It comes in handy that we have a broad practice,” said Bergh. “We have looks for the future to make it easier for ourselves to be designers.”.

“I like how they surprise with their projects and feel like we have only seen chapter one of their story,” concluded Marcelis. “And I can’t wait to discover the next chapter.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The slippery oil is squeezed out of jojoba plant seeds.
  • Though it’s been used as a natural remedy for centuries, jojoba oil is having a major hair moment right now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jojoba oil is a must-have for moisturizing shampoos and skincare products.

The slippery oil is squeezed out of jojoba plant seeds. These plants are shrubs that pop up around the desert-y spots ofArizona, southern California, and Mexico.

Though it’s been used as a natural remedy for centuries, jojoba oil is having a major hair moment right now.

Keep reading to learn how to use it for strong, shiny hair and a healthy scalp.

Recent findings suggest that “Jojoba oil is incredibly nourishing,” states Mayara Macedo, a hairstylist and scalp specialist in NYC. “It’s a natural oil that closely resembles the sebum our skin and scalp produce,” Macedo explains.

Because of this, Macedo says it’s super compatible with our bodies and works great as a balancing treatment — whether you have an oily or dry scalp.

Industry observers note that while its proven benefits mainly revolve around its help with scalp health, jojoba oil can also strengthen and moisturize hair. However, it’s not the go-to pick for improving hair loss (that’s usually minoxidil).

If you’re dealing with dryness, jojoba oil is fantastic for adding moisture to your scalp,” Macedo claims.

“Its natural hydrating properties help restore balance, leaving everything healthier and more manageable.”.

“Jojoba oil has been known for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties in addition to its conditioning and emollient properties,” claims Kseniya Kobets, MD, board-certified dermatologist and Director of Cosmetics Dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care.

These properties help out with dry, irritating dandruff.

This also explains jojoba oil‘s Mexican Indian history as a treatment for sores, which eventually caused researchers to flag its potential for improving skin conditions like acne and psoriasis (but please see a dermatologist for proven treatment options).

Though many say that jojoba oil grows hair, this claim is probably tossed around because it helps moisturize hair follicles — which can keep dryness at bay.

A dry environment can be a breeding ground for breakage, hair loss, and dandruff.

Also, your split ends say hello — jojoba oil can help by restoring hair health overall.

“If your scalp gets oily swiftly after washing,” Macedo indicates, “It could be because your scalp is overcompensating, thinking it doesn’t have enough moisture and needs to produce more oil.”.

She says adding jojoba oil helps signal to your scalp that it has enough, which can slow down excess oil production.

Although you can apply jojoba oil to the length and tips of your hair, Macedo states she prefers to use it only for the scalp, saying that other oils, like argan oil, will work better for the length.

Here;s how Macedo recommends using jojoba oil:.

You can also buy shampoos or conditions that already have it!

Macedo claims you can apply jojoba oil to wet or dry hair, depending on your goal.

“If you want to lock in moisture and add shine, you can try applying it to damp hair.” However, she doesn’t recommend this because it’s easy to accidentally apply too much or distribute it unevenly on wet hair, which she notes can leave your hair feeling heavy and greasy.

“Applying it to dry hair reduces frizz and adds a light shine to styled hair,” she suggests.

According to recent reports, kobets recommends using oils overnight for extended exposure. However, she points out this can get messy (RIP pillowcases), so you can always apply them for a few hours and wash them off before bed.

Macedo also suggests being mindful of the amount you use — too much can make your hair look greasy, especially true for fine hair. “For a lightweight finish, start with a small amount and focus on the ends of your hair. But again, I’d recommend jojoba oil for the scalp and argan oil for the hair,” Macedo adds.

“If you’re using jojoba oil as a pre-wash treatment to balance scalp oil or as a deep conditioner, apply it before washing,” Macedo explains. “If you’re using it as a leave-in conditioner or frizz-tamer, you can apply it to freshly washed hair — careful not to apply too much.”.

Kobets suggests washing the scalp after using oils, noting that her patients don’t always prefer to use them because they can reduce hair volume for some.

According to recent reports, kobets indicates that someone with a dehydrated scalp and coarse hair may want to leave the oil in to hydrate the scalp better. “People with fine or oily scalps usually want to wash the oils out,” she adds.

Recent findings suggest that jojoba oil is a natural moisturizing ingredient known for improving scalp health. It can also add shine and help strengthen your locks.

It’s not the move for improving hair loss, however.

Do a patch test to make sure you aren’t allergic first! Then you’re good to glow.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Syam Sreeshylam.

Curving ceilings sweep down to frame the two small gardens that flank this home in Kerala, India, designed by local architecture studio Fictional Project.

Named Interstitial Living, the home in the village of Adoor was designed for a family of four who wanted to feel connected to the outside, in particular the lush greenery surrounding the site.

This led Fictional Project to pull the home’s built volume back to create space for two planted yards on either side, overlooked by the home’s pared-back and open interiors.

“The residence is careful not to overpower, becoming one with the landscape,” the studio told Dezeen.

Interstitial Living is organised around a bedroom at its centre, which is housed within a cubic volume finished in cement plaster.

A small window in this bedroom overlooks a potted tree within a cut-out in the floor of the adjacent living room, which faces the yard to the west through a row of full-height windows above a built-in timber bench.

On the opposite side of the home, the kitchen overlooks the eastern yard through a row of windows above its countertops. Both these spaces are defined by the curving white-plastered ceilings overhead, which sweep down from the centre of the home.

According to recent reports, “The scale of the residence allows for intimate working spaces in the kitchen and a welcoming living room, all accentuated by the dynamic nature of the roof. The other spaces negotiate the private/public nature of the indoors,” the studio explained.

“The concavity of the roof creates a visual connection to the outdoors, becoming a marker that emerges from within the site.”.

Sources indicate that “It breaks the rigidity of a traditional sloping roof, helping create fluid indoor spaces. Nothing here is built or conceived in isolation, but rather as interconnected systems,” it added.

The smaller first floor contains a second bedroom, bathroom and a study area, which overlook the living space below from a steel-framed landing and internal windows.

While the internal finishes were kept minimal, the exterior of the home and its boundary walls were built using terracotta-toned textured blocks, which the studio described as introducing a sense of “groundedness and warmth”.

Other dwellings in Kerala recently featured on Dezeen include a home by InLe Architects framed and shaded by two large mango trees and a farmhouse by Evolving Radical Aesthetics that is built into a hillside above a carved-out, open-air temple.

Photography by Syam Sreeshylam.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Aman Group.

Fresh York studio SHoP Architects has released designs for a ribbed supertall skyscraper in Miami, revealed alongside the launch of a luxury brand for which Serbian tennis player Novak Djokovic is developing amenity facilities.

SHoP Architects, who are behind some of Newly introduced York City’s tallest buildings, designed the 1,049-foot-tall (320-metre-tall) skyscraper around ATMA, a luxury brand being rolled out by hospitality operator Aman Group.

If completed at the stated height, it would be taller than the city’s current tallest skyscraper, and have the same projected height as the in-progress Waldorf Astoria Hotel & Residences Miami, which has been cited as the city’s future tallest.

The skyscraper will include a hotel, residences and a members’ club. According to Aman Group, ATMA’s “advanced wellness programming and world-class sport facilities” will be developed “exclusively” with Djokovic, who is credited as a global partner of the upcoming brand.

Designs for the skyscraper itself show a ribbed form of balconied terraces organised around a central void that runs from the crown to the podium.

It is planned for Miami’s Brickell neighbourhood, and Aman Group said that the floor-to-ceiling windows of the skyscraper will merge the “futuristic architecture with the bay”.

Industry observers note that toronto-based interiors outfit Studio Paolo Ferrari has been chosen as the interiors lead on the project. It will include condos with one to five bedrooms, with six-bedroom penthouses pushed to the top of the skyscraper.

The structure will have setbacks at the upper floors, presumably to create more panoramic views for residences in the penthouses.

The ATMA concept is based around what Aman Group calls “performance-driven lifestyle”.

“Monolithic architecture meets biomorphic design, furniture is shaped naturally to the human form and ambience adjusts sensitively to residents’ and guests’ circadian rhythm,” noted Aman Group.

Djokovic’s programme, meanwhile, will include a 120,000-square-foot spa and wellness centre.

“ATMA Miami will sit at the pinnacle of what performance living can achieve,” stated Djokovic.

OKO Group and Oak Row Equities were unveiled as developers for the project.

SHoP Architects is no stranger to supertall luxury residences. It designed New York’s skinniest supertall skyscraper to have single-floor apartments on the city’s so-called Billionaires Row. It also designed the Brooklyn Tower, the tallest structure in the borough.

Images courtesy of Aman Group.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that your skin is your most visible organ, so it’s easy to notice when something seems off.
  • Sources indicate that many of these skin complications get better with the right at-home remedies or changes in your skin care routine.
  • According to recent reports, but if skin symptoms don’t go away with a little self-care — or they return frequently — a chronic skin condition might be the culprit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that your skin is your most visible organ, so it’s easy to notice when something seems off. It’s normal to experience some skin issues from time to time, like itchiness, breakouts, or ingrown hairs. But when these skin symptoms stick around, it could be a sign that something more serious is going on.

Sources indicate that many of these skin complications get better with the right at-home remedies or changes in your skin care routine. For example, if dryness pops up when Old Man Winter comes along, slathering on a more intense moisturizer may help.

According to recent reports, but if skin symptoms don’t go away with a little self-care — or they return frequently — a chronic skin condition might be the culprit. However, just because you have a lasting symptom or two doesn’t necessarily mean you have a chronic health concern.

In a recent development, here are the symptoms you should watch for and what they might mean. And if they don’t improve, consider checking in with a dermatologist for a proper diagnosis and a strategy of action.

In a recent development, if you wish you had cat claws to satisfy your skin itch, you could be dealing with eczema. Eczema is an umbrella term for several conditions that impact the skin, with atopic dermatitis being the most common.

With most forms of eczema, your skin may show signs of inflammation, such as:.

These symptoms may flare up occasionally and then go into periods of remission, where your skin isn’t as irritated.

Allergies can also lead to itchiness. For example, if you’re allergic to a skin care ingredient, a fabric type, a pet, or another allergen, your skin might react as a way to tell you to avoid this trigger.

Ongoing or regular periods of itchiness are a reason to see a dermatologist.

A rash can affect the skin in various ways, including:.

A one-off or temporary rash might result from friction or chafing from a upcoming outfit item. It could also be a heat rash when sweat gets trapped in skinfolds or bodily creases.

A persistent rash could be a sign of eczema or allergies. However, different types of rashes can be a sign of other things. For example, a butterfly-shaped (malar) rash across the face is a common sign of an autoimmune disease known as lupus.

If you frequently experience skin rashes, talk with a dermatologist to help you get to the bottom of the glitch.

Sources indicate that dry skin can be just that — dry skin. Common causes include:.

But if your skin is so dry it makes you want to bathe in a vat of thick moisturizer, it could be a sign of psoriasis.

It has been revealed that psoriasis is an inflammatory skin condition potentially caused by an overactive immune system. It can lead to dry, cracked, or scaling skin. In fact, psoriasis often involves a buildup of scales or plaques on areas like the elbows or knees — though they can occur anywhere.

Psoriasis and eczema are different conditions, but they have overlapping symptoms that mimic each other. So if you experience these symptoms, it’s notable to see a dermatologist to identify and treat the underlying cause.

Changes in skin color — including red, brown, gray, or purple patches of skin — can be a sign of various skin problems, including eczema, psoriasis, or allergies. But it can also be a sign of rosacea.

Rosacea typically involves persistent redness that looks like a sunburn or blushing. It may also lead to skin thickening.

Recent findings suggest that the good news? Rosacea is highly treatable. So working with a dermatologist can help you address it.

No one is immune from developing the occasional pimple or ingrown hair. But sometimes, skin bumps can be a sign that something else is going on.

Acne is one of the most common skin conditions that could bring skin bumps like pimples.

According to recent reports, hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is another condition that causes painful, boil-like lumps to form underneath the skin. These bumps can turn into pus-filled pockets that may connect via tunnels. HS typically demonstrates up in areas of high friction or where skin meets skin, such as the armpits or groin.

Other types of skin bumps may include ingrown hairs, which can get infected and turn into folliculitis.

Talk with a dermatologist to help you address any bothersome skin bumps you may experience.

Common moles are growths that develop when pigment cells (melanocytes) grow in clusters. The average adult has between 10 to 40 common moles.

In a recent development, an irregular mole, also known as a dysplastic nevus, is a type of mole that looks different from your common moles. If you have a dysplastic nevus (or several), schedule regular skin checks with a dermatologist to look for anything suspicious. Be sure to mention any changes in:.

Industry observers note that these types of changes could be a sign of a form of skin cancer such as melanoma, which occurs in melanocytes. Melanoma can develop anywhere, including on normal-looking skin, a common mole, or a dysplastic nevus.

In a recent development, skin symptoms — like rashes, bumps, discoloration, dryness, or itchiness — may come and go. But if symptoms stick around or return frequently, consider seeing a dermatologist for an evaluation. Your skin may be telling you that there’s an underlying issue that needs to be addressed.

A dermatologist can provide a proper diagnosis and treatment plan to help reduce, or, in some cases, resolve your skin symptoms. If you don’t currently have a dermatologist, your primary care physician or nurse practitioner can refer you to one.

  • The Montreal-based studio recently unveiled The Clayfield Hotel, a 60-room hotel with a restaurant, ballroom and rooftop terrace in Niagara-on-the-Lake.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by James Brittain (unless stated otherwise).

Canadian studio Sid Lee Architecture has created a curved-glass hotel that takes cues from the burgeoning wine region of Ontario.

The Montreal-based studio recently unveiled The Clayfield Hotel, a 60-room hotel with a restaurant, ballroom and rooftop terrace in Niagara-on-the-Lake.

The rounded 94,000-square-foot (8,732-square metre) hotel sits on a property in the historic village that is being transformed by winemakers.

“The Clayfield was conceived as a latest hub for Niagara-on-the-Lake, a place where wine culture and hospitality find a home,” Martin Leblanc, architect and co-founding partner of Sid Lee Architecture, told Dezeen.

“Its layered contours, rounded geometry and rhythmic wood elements translate the surrounding vineyard landscape into a building that celebrates the region’s contribution to Canadian winemaking.”.

The hotel was conceived as a pavilion set in the emerging townscape between vineyards and the Clayfield Commons housing development on an agricultural road.

The curved form allows access and connection to its surroundings in multiple directions.

“The hotel acts as a threshold between these typologies, connecting the vineyard and the denser village-like development around it,” Leblanc noted.

“Its exterior wood elements recall the rhythm of the vine rows, the layered concrete refers to the clay soil and the reflective glass registers the changing light, sky and seasons.”.

The studio said that the organic, natural flow of a hotel is essential to the lasting success of the design.

Working back and forth between the architecture and the interior design, the studio laid out spaces to progress from public to private and back again, integrating moments for visitors to discover the landscape.

Sources indicate that “As visitors approach and circulate around the building, it frames changing views of the vines, the plaza and the emerging neighbourhood,” Leblanc said. “The lobby acts as a gateway to the vineyard, while the rooftop terrace reconnects the hotel experience with its broader surroundings.”.

Meanwhile, the staircase acts as a connector, transition and centrepiece between the plaza, lobby and upper levels.

“Inside, we chose a palette that speaks to the natural beauty of Niagara’s wine country: walnut panelling, concrete, dark amaranth-coloured leather, greige limestone and woven fabrics,” Leblanc said, calling out the limestone registration desk chiselled from the Niagara Escarpment and the restaurant’s curved bar that resembles the shape of the building.

With mostly Teknion furniture, each space represents a season of the vineyard, from spring in the lobby to winter in the guest rooms with more quiet, reserved furnishings that complete the rooms that fan out from the rounded concrete strata.

Industry observers note that founded in 2009, Sid Lee Architecture has six offices across North America and Europe. The studio previously remodelled its own offices in an I.M. Pei office building, overhauled the interiors of the iconic Fairmont Queen Elizabeth Hotel and created an artisan-inspired workplace for video game designers – all in Montreal.
